title: How to Construct Domain Specific LLM Evaluation Systems: Hamel Husain and Emil Sedgh

summary:
Emil Sedgh, CTO at Rechat, describes building Lucy, an AI personal assistant for real estate agents handling tasks like creating contacts, sending emails, finding listings, and creating websites. After prototyping with GPT 3.5 and the React framework, the team achieved an impressive demo but struggled to move to production because they had no way to measure whether changes were improvements—each prompt modification risked breaking other use cases, leaving them "essentially in the dark."

Hamel Husain presents a systematic evaluation approach. The foundation is unit tests and assertions based on observed failure modes (e.g., emails not sent, invalid placeholders). These are cheap, provide immediate feedback, and should run in CI with results logged to existing tools (Rechat used Metabase). He strongly advises against buying new tools prematurely—you must understand the process manually before adopting tools, otherwise you cannot evaluate them. The next layer is logging traces and human review; he stresses building custom data viewing and annotation apps to remove friction, since domain-specific traces require domain-specific filtering. Removing all friction from data review is described as the most important takeaway.

For test case generation, LLMs can synthetically generate inputs by role-playing as real estate agents. The minimal eval system—unit tests, trace logging, human review—should be validated through a prompt engineering loop, unlocking fine-tuning data curation as a near-free superpower. Hamel introduces LLM-as-a-judge for cases not expressible as assertions, emphasizing alignment with human judgment through iterative spreadsheet-based labeling. He identifies common mistakes: not looking at data, focusing on tools rather than processes, using generic off-the-shelf evals (conciseness, toxicity scores) as a crutch, and adopting LLM-as-a-judge too early.

Emil reports that implementing this framework rapidly increased the LLM application's success rate—something previously seeming impossible. He explains why fine-tuning was necessary despite few-shot prompting and smarter agents: Lucy needed to mix natural language with UI elements (structured and unstructured output together), handle feedback loops where the agent asks for more input, and execute complex multi-tool commands. He demonstrates a complex command where the agent finds listings by criteria, creates a website, renders an Instagram post video, prepares an email, invites someone to dinner, and creates a follow-up task—work that could take a non-savvy real estate agent hours, completed in a minute.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Product Context
sections.summary: Emil Sedgh introduces himself and Rechat's AI assistant Lucy, built for real estate agents. He describes the initial prototype built with GPT 3.5 and React—slow and error-prone but impressive when it worked—prompting the push toward production.

sections.title: The Improvement Challenge Without Evaluation
sections.summary: Emil describes the core problem: without evaluation, the team couldn't measure success or failure rates after changes. Prompt modifications risked breaking other use cases, leaving them 'essentially in the dark.' He introduces Hamel as a partner to help make the app production-ready.

sections.title: Unit Tests and Assertions as Foundation
sections.summary: Hamel explains that unit tests and assertions based on observed failure modes are the essential foundation of an eval system. They provide immediate feedback, are nearly free to run, and should be executed in CI with results logged to existing tools like Metabase. He strongly advises against jumping straight to LLM-as-a-judge or buying new tools when starting out.

sections.title: Logging, Traces, and Human Review
sections.summary: Hamel covers logging traces (Rechat used LangSmith) and stresses that looking at data is the most important part. He advocates building custom data viewing and annotation apps to remove friction, since domain-specific traces need domain-specific filtering. Any friction in data review will destroy the entire process.

sections.title: Synthetic Data, Eval Workflow, and Fine-Tuning Superpower
sections.summary: Hamel explains using LLMs to synthetically generate test inputs by role-playing as users. The minimal eval system should be validated through a prompt engineering loop. He notes that the eval framework unlocks fine-tuning data curation as a near-free superpower, reducing human review costs over time as more is automated.

sections.title: LLM-as-a-Judge and Common Mistakes
sections.summary: Hamel introduces LLM-as-a-judge for cases not expressible as assertions, emphasizing alignment with human judgment through iterative spreadsheet-based labeling with domain experts. He identifies common mistakes: not looking at data, focusing on tools rather than processes, using generic off-the-shelf evals as a crutch, and adopting LLM-as-a-judge too early.

sections.title: Common Mistakes: Tools, Generic Evals, and Early LLM-as-a-Judge
sections.summary: Hamel elaborates on common mistakes: adopting tools before understanding the process manually, using generic off-the-shelf evals (conciseness, toxicity scores) as a crutch, and jumping to LLM-as-a-judge too early. He notes that close data inspection often reveals sufficient assertions and failure modes without needing LLM-as-a-judge.

sections.title: Results and Why Fine-Tuning Was Necessary
sections.summary: Emil reports rapid success-rate improvements after implementing the eval framework. He explains why fine-tuning was required despite few-shot prompting and smarter agents: Lucy needed to mix natural language with UI elements (structured and unstructured output), handle feedback loops, and execute complex multi-tool commands. He demonstrates a command where the agent finds listings, creates a website, renders an Instagram post, prepares an email, invites someone to dinner, and creates a follow-up task—work that could take a non-savvy agent hours, done in a minute.
